title: EHR Basics and Master Patient Index

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the purpose of an electronic health record and its benefits for patient care and office operations.
- Explain the function of the master patient index in uniquely identifying patients and preventing duplicate or mixed records.
- Identify the dimensions of data quality (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, consistency) and explain why they matter for patient safety.
- Recognize the medical office assistant's role in accurate data entry, verification, and correction, including escalation of discrepancies to licensed staff.
- Apply HIPAA privacy and security principles, including the minimum necessary standard, access controls, and patient rights, when handling EHR data.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An EHR is like a secure digital notebook about a patient's health that all the doctors and nurses who are allowed can open and add to, instead of loose papers in a folder.

### Question 2

It is like many people reading the same online document at once, instead of only one person holding a paper file at a time.

### Question 3

Typing words clearly is like printing instead of writing messy cursive, so everyone can read it correctly.

### Question 4

An EHR is a shared, secure file so everyone helping the patient sees the same important notes.

### Question 5

It is like a spell-checker that flags a possible problem so the writer can decide what to do about it.

### Question 6

It is like a diary of a patient's health that keeps all the past pages, so each visit does not start from scratch.

### Question 7

PHI is a patient's private information, like a secret that only the people helping them should know.

### Question 8

It is like a locker room where only the people who need a certain key can open that locker.

### Question 9

An EMR is like a notebook kept in one office; an EHR is like a shared folder the whole care team can use.

### Question 10

It is like pulling up the right page in the right notebook rather than guessing.

### Question 11

It is like a long timeline of someone's health, with all the important events lined up in order.

### Question 12

It is like checking a shared photo album so no one takes the same picture twice.

### Question 13

It is like a scoreboard that collects everyone's results so the team can see how to improve.

### Question 14

It is like keeping a receipt for every purchase so the bill matches what actually happened.

### Question 15

It is like sending a typed, spell-checked message instead of a hard-to-read note.

### Question 16

It is like not loaning your house key to someone who does not need to be inside.

### Question 17

It is like a sign-in sheet that shows who opened a file and when.

### Question 18

It is like each player having their own jersey number so you know who did what.

### Question 19

It is like taking only the one tool you need from the toolbox instead of emptying the whole box.

### Question 20

It is like saving a copy of your homework in two places so it is not lost if the computer breaks.

### Question 21

It is like a library's card catalog that tells you exactly which book belongs to which person and where to find it.

### Question 22

It is like making sure each person has one and only one name tag so their things do not get mixed up.

### Question 23

It is like using someone's full name and birthday, not their favorite color, to tell them apart.

### Question 24

It is like checking the guest list before writing a new name tag so no one gets two tags.

### Question 25

If you find two folders for the same person, you ask a manager to combine them carefully rather than throwing one away.

### Question 26

It is like putting someone else's pages into your notebook by mistake, so both of your notes get jumbled together.

### Question 27

If your name tag shows the wrong birthday, you ask to have it fixed properly rather than just scribbling over it.

### Question 28

It is like giving each student a different ID number so two students named Sam do not get confused.

### Question 29

Always check whether someone already has a name tag before making a new one.

### Question 30

Two classmates named Sam can be told apart by their birthdays, not their favorite colors.

### Question 31

It is like updating a library card with a new name but keeping the same borrower account.

### Question 32

It is like checking that your contact card is still correct each time you visit.

### Question 33

Combining two folders must be done carefully by someone trained, so nothing important is lost.

### Question 34

The MPI is like the label on a file cabinet drawer telling you which drawer holds which person's files.

### Question 35

Sending someone else's test result to the wrong name tag could mean the wrong person gets the wrong care.

### Question 36

An ID number is like a fingerprint for records, no two people share it.

### Question 37

If unsure which locker is yours, check more clues carefully rather than opening a random one.

### Question 38

The people who write the name tags are responsible for keeping them correct.

### Question 39

It is like one master guest list used by every branch of a big hotel chain.

### Question 40

The right name tag means the right medicine and results go to the right person.

### Question 41

Accurate means 'right', like writing down the correct spelling of a friend's name.

### Question 42

A complete form is one where every important question is answered, not left blank.

### Question 43

It is writing down today's weather today, not next month, so the note is useful now.

### Question 44

It is writing a friend's name the same way every time so you do not create two different-looking names.

### Question 45

It is like rules that keep an important shared document from being changed or erased by the wrong people.

### Question 46

Always check the exact spelling on someone's ID so their name tag is right.

### Question 47

If two labels show different birthdays, check which one is right before fixing it.

### Question 48

It is like repeating a phone number back to be sure you wrote it down correctly.

### Question 49

Never fill in a blank with a guess; ask the person who knows.

### Question 50

If you write something wrong in a shared notebook, fix it properly and tell the right person.

### Question 51

It is like being able to ask that a mistake in your file be corrected, and if they disagree, you can add your side.

### Question 52

If you spot a mistake in the teacher's notes, you tell the teacher rather than erasing it yourself.

### Question 53

Write down what actually happened or was said, not what you think about the person.

### Question 54

It is better to write 'don't know yet' than to make up an answer.

### Question 55

Choosing from a menu is easier and safer than writing the same word ten different ways.

### Question 56

Writing down the wrong allergy is like telling the kitchen someone is fine with nuts when they are not.

### Question 57

Listing the same medicine twice is like counting it twice by accident.

### Question 58

Structured data is like checkboxes; free text is like a paragraph. Checkboxes are easier to count.

### Question 59

Use two clues, like a name and a birthday, to be sure you have the right person.

### Question 60

If two versions of an important note do not match, ask a supervisor to sort it out.

### Question 61

Getting the basics right (name, birthday, address) makes everything else work.

### Question 62

Check your contact card each visit in case the address or phone changed.

### Question 63

The MOA keeps the notebook organized; the doctors and nurses decide the medical answers.

### Question 64

Update the address so packages go to the right house.

### Question 65

Keep your homework answers covered so others cannot peek.

### Question 66

Lock your locker when you leave so no one else opens it with your name.

### Question 67

If your notebook page tears, you tell the teacher and rewrite the notes.

### Question 68

Take only the one folder you need, not the whole cabinet.

### Question 69

You learn the rules of a game before you play, so everyone stays safe.

### Question 70

Check twice before you write down something really important.

### Question 71

You have a right to see your own report card and ask for a copy.

### Question 72

It is like a welcome letter explaining the rules about keeping your information private.

### Question 73

PHI is health information with your name on it that should stay private.

### Question 74

A name or ID number makes information 'about you'; a wall color does not.

### Question 75

The clinic can use your information to treat you and bill your insurance without a special permission slip each time.

### Question 76

Sharing your information for a reason outside your care needs a permission slip.

### Question 77

It is like a company hired to safely store your things, with a signed promise to keep them safe.

### Question 78

A breach is when private information gets out when it should not have.

### Question 79

A password is a technical lock on the digital file.

### Question 80

You are allowed a copy of your own report card when you ask.

### Question 81

If a note seems to be in the wrong locker, stop and check before using it.

### Question 82

It is taking the name off a test so no one knows whose it is.

### Question 83

A typo in an ID number needs to be fixed carefully, not covered up with a new number.

### Question 84

Even when you are in a hurry, double-checking keeps the wrong name tag off the wrong person.

### Question 85

The MOA can pass along questions to the doctor, who is the one who explains the answers.
